“Mañjuśrī! What is the spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas? Mañjuśrī!

It is, for example, as if in each of the ten directions, beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in the dust of fifty oceans of worlds—worlds numbering as many as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas—in all those worlds, in every single world, and in every single Jambudvīpa, one were to see the form-body (*rūpakāya*) of the Buddha in every moment of thought, seeing it all at once rather than seeing it sequentially.”

Yet the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not engage in conceptualization and are free from conceptualization; they are spontaneously thus. Being without conceptualization and free from conceptualization, they are spontaneously thus, perceiving everything simultaneously and universally.
Why is this? Because they have attained correspondence with the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). "Mañjuśrī!..."

Beyond fifty oceans of world-microdust worlds in each of the ten directions—worlds as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya worlds—in all these worlds, and in every single Jambudvīpa within each world, at every moment of thought, the natural wisdom of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, spontaneously manifests according to the various roots of goodness and various practices of sentient beings, as well as through all their diverse and manifold arts and crafts.

Yet the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not engage in discrimination and are free from discrimination; they are naturally thus, without discrimination and free from discrimination, and it is by this natural state that all arts and crafts are manifested.
Why is this? Because they have attained correspondence with the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). "Mañjuśrī!..."

In the worlds of the ten directions, in all oceans of worlds, and in all places of abode—whether mundane or supramundane—all dharmas are accomplished; all such matters of every kind spontaneously appear before all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Why is this? Because they have attained correspondence with the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma). "Mañjuśrī!..."

For example, just as the great earth, by virtue of depending upon the earth, sustains all seeds, grasses, shrubs, and forests, enabling them to grow and flourish, and bringing them to full completion—whether broad or narrow, large or small.

Yet that great earth is without discrimination and free from discrimination; it is naturally thus, without discrimination and free from discrimination, naturally thus, growing and expanding, whether broad or narrow, large or small, all brought to completion.
Why is this? Because they have attained correspondence with the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). "Mañjuśrī!..."

In this way, based upon the sustaining power of the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, throughout the oceans of world-systems in the ten directions, there arise the various activities of non-Buddhists, Nirgranthas, and others, as well as the roots of goodness and karmic deeds of all sentient beings—whether mundane or supramundane—and their growth, expansion, contraction, and the accomplishment of both great and small results.

Yet all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are without discrimination and free from discrimination, being naturally thus; they are without discrimination and free from discrimination, being naturally thus, as they grow, expand, contract, and achieve their great or small forms.
Why is this? Because they have attained correspondence with the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). "Mañjuśrī!..."

For example, suppose there is a person who arrives at a place where medicinal herbs grow free from thorns; all the thorns fall away of their own accord. Yet that place does not conceptualize or engage in discrimination, but is naturally so—without conceptualization or discrimination, it is naturally so—and thus the thorns and medicinal herbs all fall away.
Why is this? Because they have attained correspondence with the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma). "Mañjuśrī!..."
In this way, all these sentient beings, even unto those who have fully understood all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, or who possess the caskets of the sūtras—
by virtue of that cause, all the thorns of greed, hatred, and delusion within those sentient beings shall completely fall away.

Yet the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not discriminate and are free from discrimination; they are naturally thus, without discrimination and free from discrimination, naturally thus, so that the thorns of greed, hatred, and delusion all fall away.
Why is this? Because they have attained correspondence with the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). "Mañjuśrī!..."

For example, it is like the king of wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*): whatever sentient beings may require, it can provide it all. Yet the king of wish-fulfilling jewels does not discriminate or engage in discrimination; it is naturally so, without discrimination or engagement in discrimination, being naturally such that it can provide whatever is required by all.
Why is this? Because it is associated with the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma). "Mañjuśrī!

In this way, whether it be humans, devas, or bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who go to the presence of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, desiring to hear and contemplate such and such teachings and their meanings, all those humans and devas shall fully hear each and every dharma they seek.

Yet the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not conceptualize and are free from conceptualization; they are naturally thus, without conceptualization and free from conceptualization, being naturally thus, so that all beings are able to hear each of those various teachings.
Why is this? Because they have attained correspondence with the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma). “Mañjuśrī!

This is called a brief explanation of the unobstructed wisdom of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas; were it to be explained in detail, it could not be fully recounted even if one were to remain for as many eons as there are until the end of the future.
“Mañjuśrī! What is the inconceivable realm of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas? Mañjuśrī!”
Regarding the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas: throughout the worlds of the ten directions, in every single world, within every atom, and in each and every atom, they enter the oceans of all worlds;
and it is likewise for every world within those atomic worlds, and for every Jambudvīpa within each of those worlds.

"Mañjuśrī! Beyond oceans of world-microdusts as numerous as the microdusts of fifty worlds, there are oceans of various and diverse merit-adornments belonging to Buddha-Tathāgatas as numerous as the microdusts of incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of worlds. These possess incalculable varieties of Dharma-teachings with diverse distinctions, which are manifested in every thought-moment as unobstructed, unhindered, and undifferentiated, pervading the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm without limit, remaining for the duration of all kalpas until the end of the future."

"In this way, this great ocean adorned with the merits of various and diverse forms of wisdom contains incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) and distinct methods of teaching and distinct classifications; in every thought-moment, it manifests without obstruction, without hindrance, and without differentiation, pervading the entirety of space and the dharma-realm, reaching no limit, and remaining for as many eons as there are until the end of the future."

“In this way, these various and diverse oceans of *pāramitās* possess incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) diverse teachings and diverse distinctions; moment by moment they manifest without obstruction, without hindrance, and without differentiation, pervading the entirety of space and the *dharmadhātu*, reaching no limit, and remaining for the duration of all kalpas until the end of the future.”

"In this way, within these various and diverse oceans of dwelling grounds, there are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) different teachings and different distinctions, which are manifested in every thought-moment as unobstructed, unhindered, and undifferentiated, pervading the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) without limit, remaining as a sustaining power throughout all kalpas until the end of the future."

"In this way, within these various and diverse great oceans of dhāraṇīs, there are incalculable (asaṃkhyeya) distinct methods of teaching and distinct differences; moment by moment they manifest without obstruction, without hindrance, and without differentiation, pervading the entirety of space and the dharma-realm, reaching no limit, and remaining for as many eons as exist until the end of the future."

"In this way, within these various and diverse great oceans of samādhi, there are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) diverse methods of teaching and diverse distinctions; moment by moment they are manifested without obstruction, without hindrance, and without differentiation, pervading the entirety of space and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), reaching no limit, and remaining for the duration of all kalpas until the end of the future."

"In this way, within these various and diverse great oceans of liberation, there are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) distinct methods of teaching and distinct differences, which are manifested in every thought-moment as unobstructed, unhindered, and undifferentiated, pervading the entirety of space and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), without limit, and remaining for all kalpas until the end of the future."

"Such a great ocean of various and diverse unhindered eloquence possesses incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) diverse modes of teaching the Dharma and diverse distinctions; in every thought-moment it manifests without obstruction, without hindrance, and without differentiation, pervading the entirety of space and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), reaching no limit, and remaining for as many eons as there are until the end of the future."

"Thus, within this great ocean of various and diverse vows, there are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) different modes of teaching and different distinctions, which are manifested in every thought-moment as unobstructed, unhindered, and undifferentiated, pervading the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm without limit, remaining and sustaining them throughout all kalpas until the end of the future."

"In this way, within these various and diverse oceans of peace and security, there are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) different teachings and different distinctions, which moment by moment manifest without obstruction, without hindrance, and without differentiation, pervading the entirety of space and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), reaching no limit, and remaining for as many eons as there are until the end of the future."

"In this way, there are various and diverse ways of entering the great ocean of bodhisattva practices, with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) diverse teachings and diverse distinctions. Moment by moment, they are manifested without obstruction, without hindrance, and without differentiation, pervading the entirety of space and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), reaching no limit, and remaining for as many eons as exist until the end of the future."

"In this way, there are various and diverse means of entry into the great ocean of the Tathāgata; there are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) diverse teachings and diverse distinctions, manifested in every thought-moment as unobstructed, unimpeded, and undifferentiated, pervading the entirety of space and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) without limit, remaining for the duration of all kalpas until the end of the future."

In this way, there are various and diverse means of entry that accord with the ocean-like mental activities of sentient beings; there are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) diverse teachings and diverse distinctions, which moment by moment manifest without obstruction, without hindrance, and without differentiation, pervading the entirety of space and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), reaching no limit, and remaining for the duration of all kalpas until the end of the future.

“In this way, within the great ocean of worlds where various and diverse beings enter, there are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) and distinct methods of teaching the Dharma with various differences; in every thought-moment, they manifest without obstruction, without hindrance, and without distinction, pervading the entirety of space and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), reaching no limit and remaining for as many eons as exist until the end of the future.”

"In this way, there are various and diverse great oceans of eons for entering [the path], with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) diverse methods of teaching the Dharma and diverse distinctions. Moment by moment, they manifest without obstruction, without hindrance, and without differentiation, pervading the entirety of space and the dharma-realm, reaching no limit, and remaining sustained throughout all future eons."

“Mañjuśrī! In the worlds of the ten directions, in all worlds—the great ocean of worlds of the past, future, and present—all the Tathāgata Buddhas manifest within every single pore, and within each and every pore, at one and the same time, not sequentially.”
Why is this? Because it has attained that which is without limit and without middle. "Mañjuśrī!

This is called a brief explanation of the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas; if it were to be explained in detail, it could not be exhausted even if one were to remain for as many eons as there are until the end of the future.
“Mañjuśrī! How do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, see universally? Mañjuśrī!”

Regarding the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas: throughout the worlds of the ten directions, within all worlds, they see sentient beings as they pass away, as they are born, as they enter the good realms, or as they enter the evil realms. Thus do they see them with the mark of the uṣṇīṣa on the Tathāgata’s crown; thus do they see them with the mark of the white tuft (ūrṇā-kośa) between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows; thus do they see each and every one of the Tathāgata’s primary marks (lakṣaṇa); thus do they see each and every one of the Tathāgata’s secondary signs (anuvyañjana); and thus do they see each and every one of the Tathāgata’s pores.
In this way, at one and the same time—without seeing them sequentially—he beholds all worlds, observing sentient beings as they pass away, are reborn, enter the good realms, or enter the evil realms.

“Mañjuśrī! This is called a brief explanation of the universal vision of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas; were it to be explained in detail, it could not be fully expressed even if one were to remain for as many eons as there are until the end of the future.
“Mañjuśrī! What is the renown of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas? Mañjuśrī!”

That which is called the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, enter into all worlds throughout the ten directions—every single world, every single Jambudvīpa, every single atom, and all worlds within every atom, into the ocean of all worlds.

In this manner, in each and every world, in each and every Jambudvīpa, within every moment of thought, he manifests with vigor for as many sentient beings as there are atoms in all worlds—unobstructed, unhindered, and without distinction—pervading the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm without limit, remaining to sustain and guide those beings who can be transformed until the end of all future kalpas.

Why is this? Because they have attained correspondence with the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), there is such a display of power in the Buddha-field, such a display of power in the body, and such a display of power in their vows.

Such is the mastery of objective realms, such is the mastery of wisdom, such is the mastery of supernormal powers, and such is the mastery of powers; in each and every thought-moment, there are as many such masteries as there are atoms in all worlds. These are manifested without obstruction, without hindrance, and without distinction, pervading the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm to its infinite limits, remaining for the sustenance of those beings capable of being transformed until the end of all future kalpas.
Why is this? Because they have attained correspondence with the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). "Mañjuśrī!..."

This is called a brief explanation of the names of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas; if explained in detail, even if one were to abide for as many eons as there are until the end of the future, they could not be fully recounted.
“Mañjuśrī! How is it that all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are without differentiation and without dependence? Mañjuśrī!”
What is called the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, does not possess differentiation within this world, nor is there any lack of differentiation in other worlds. Mañjuśrī!
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not rely upon this world, nor do they rely upon other worlds.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not differ in this Jambudvīpa; they are no different in other Jambudvīpas. Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not rely upon this Jambudvīpa, nor do they rely upon other Jambudvīpas.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not rely upon the distinctions of this realm of animals, nor do they rely upon the lack of distinction in other realms of animals.
Mañjuśrī! For the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, there is no distinction among these various hungry ghost realms, nor is there any distinction among other hungry ghost realms. Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not rely upon this animal realm, nor do they rely upon other animal realms.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not rely upon the distinctions of the desire realm or the form realm.

“Mañjuśrī! This is a brief explanation of the non-differentiation and non-reliance of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas; were it to be explained in detail, even if one were to abide for as many eons as there are until the end of the future, it could not be fully told. “Mañjuśrī! [he continued.]
"How is it that the bodies of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are without obstruction? 'Mañjuśrī!

It is because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in all worlds throughout the ten directions—the great oceans of lands and all dwelling places—and for all infinite sentient beings of the three periods of time, act according to the minds of those beings and according to their capacity for transformation. In every moment of thought, they manifest the arising and ceasing of dharmas from the mark of the uṣṇīṣa on their heads, such that beings may see, hear, and know them according to what they ought to perceive. Thus, while empty space may allow for universal vision, the uṣṇīṣa-mark of the Tathāgata can never be seen.'"

In this way, throughout the ten directions, across all worlds and the great oceans of lands, in every dwelling place and throughout the boundless three periods of time, for all sentient beings, according to their minds and according to what they may be transformed by, in every moment of thought, within all the marks and signs of excellence, and within each individual mark and sign, and within all the pores of the skin, and within each individual pore, the Tathāgata manifests the arising and ceasing of dharmic appearances. He causes them to see, hear, and know exactly as those sentient beings ought to see, hear, and know. While it might be possible for empty space to be seen everywhere, the appearance of even a single pore of a Buddha-Tathāgata can never be fully seen.

Just as devas, humans, and bodhisattvas, in accordance with the minds of sentient beings and according to their capacity for transformation, teach by relying on the characteristics of arising and ceasing, causing them to enter into the Dharma through whatever they can believe.

“Mañjuśrī! There may be gods, humans, or bodhisattvas who see the Tathāgata’s crown-mark emitting an ocean of adornments of incalculable merit and expounding various teachings; they understand such dharmas and explain them for the sake of sentient beings, causing sentient beings to hear them and enter into the Dharma according to their respective inclinations.”
There are some sentient beings who know the great ocean of various teachings adorned with the merit of incalculable wisdom;
there are some sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme teaching of the great ocean of incalculable perfections;
and there are some sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme teaching of the great ocean of incalculable stages of abiding.
There are some sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme teaching of the great ocean of incalculable dhāraṇīs;
there are some sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme teaching of the great ocean of incalculable samādhis;
and there are some sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme teaching of the great ocean of incalculable liberations.
There are some sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme Dharma teaching of the great ocean of incalculable, unimpeded, and joyful eloquence;
there are some sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme Dharma teaching of the great ocean of incalculable supernormal powers;
and there are some sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme Dharma teaching of the great ocean of incalculable exertion of diligent vigor.
There are some sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme Dharma-teaching that leads to the great ocean of attaining peace for incalculable [aeons];
there are some sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme Dharma-teaching that causes entry into the great ocean of bodhisattva practices for incalculable [aeons];
and there are some sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme Dharma-teaching that causes entry into the great ocean of the Tathāgatas for incalculable [aeons].
There are some sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme teaching that causes them to enter the ocean of the mental activities of immeasurable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings;
there are some sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme teaching that causes them to enter the ocean of immeasurable worlds;
and there are some sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme teaching that causes them to enter the ocean of immeasurable eons.
There may be sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme teaching that causes entry into the great ocean of the incalculable [teachings] regarding the three periods of time;
there may be sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme teaching that causes entry into the great ocean of the incalculable teachings regarding the three periods of time;
and there may be sentient beings who hear the sound of the supreme teaching that causes entry into the great ocean of the incalculable mind of tirelessness.

There may be devas or bodhisattvas who, seeing from the uṣṇīṣa of the Buddha’s crown the emergence of a great ocean of incalculable, non-differentiated wisdom that expounds various teachings, understand such dharmas and explain them for the sake of sentient beings, causing sentient beings to hear them and enter into the Dharma according to their respective inclinations.

"In this way, in every thought-moment, regarding all the marks and signs, each individual mark and sign, all the pores, each individual pore—likewise throughout the worlds of the ten directions, all worlds, and each individual world—according to the minds of sentient beings and according to those who may be transformed, devas, humans, and bodhisattvas see from a single pore of the Buddha-Tathāgata emerge an incalculable number of various oceans of Dharma and various preachings of the Dharma. They know these Dharmas and preach them for the sake of sentient beings, causing sentient beings to hear them; according to their respective faiths, they enter into the Dharma."

“Mañjuśrī! This is called a brief explanation of the unobstructed body of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas; were it to be explained in detail, even if one were to abide for as many eons as there are until the end of the future, it could not be fully described.”
“Mañjuśrī! Why is it that the uṣṇīṣa of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, cannot be seen? Mañjuśrī!”

Mañjuśrī! What are called the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are beyond oceans of world-dust particles equal in number to the dust motes of fifty worlds; they are oceans of great assemblies of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and Mahāsattvas, as numerous as the dust motes of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas.

Thus, Mañjuśrī, there are oceans of worlds as numerous as the atoms in fifty world-systems, and oceans of great assemblies of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and Mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of worlds.
There may be bodhisattvas who see the Tathāgata’s body as one hundred yojanas in height;
there may be bodhisattvas who see it as ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or one hundred yojanas in height;
likewise, there may be bodhisattvas who see the Tathāgata’s body as one hundred yojanas in height.
There were some bodhisattvas who saw [the assembly] at a height of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or a hundred yojanas;
some bodhisattvas saw it at a height of a thousand yojanas right there in that great assembly;
and some bodhisattvas saw it at a height of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or a hundred thousand yojanas.
In this way, some bodhisattvas saw [the Tathāgata’s body] rising to a height of one thousand yojanas within that very great assembly;
some bodhisattvas saw it rising to a height of ten, twenty, thirty, or forty thousand yojanas;
and some bodhisattvas saw the Tathāgata’s body reaching a height of one billion yojanas.
There may be bodhisattvas who see [the Tathāgata’s body] as ten, twenty, thirty, or forty billion yojanas in height.
Likewise, there may be bodhisattvas who see the Tathāgata’s body as one hundred million yojanas in height;
or there may be bodhisattvas who see it as ten, twenty, thirty, or forty billion yojanas in height.
There may be some bodhisattvas who see the Tathāgata’s body as being one thousand billion yojanas in height;
there may be some bodhisattvas who see it as ten, twenty, thirty, or forty thousand billion yojanas in height.
In all world-oceans and lands throughout the ten directions, and in every Jambudvīpa, the Tathāgata is seen simultaneously by all, not seen sequentially.

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in the samādhi of inconceivable liberation; in every thought-moment, he takes a single step equal to fifty world-systems as numerous as the atoms within a world-system. As he travels toward the eastern worlds, with each single step he passes through oceans of world-systems as numerous as the atoms in fifty world-systems, proceeding toward the east. Desiring to observe the crown-mark of the Tathāgata, he proceeds in this manner for an ocean of eons as numerous as the atoms in fifty world-systems until he reaches that place; yet, when he observes the crown-mark of the Tathāgata, it appears twice as high as before.”
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has attained the association with the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma). "Mañjuśrī!..."

This is called a brief explanation of the Tathāgata’s uṣṇīṣa being unobservable; were it to be explained in detail, even if one were to abide for as many eons as there are until the end of the future, it could not be fully described.
“Mañjuśrī! How do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, sustain the bodhisattva practices and teach and transform sentient beings? Mañjuśrī!”

Regarding the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas: even the worlds in the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms within them, are still but a small number; for the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, exceed that number, performing acts of teaching and transformation in all worlds, in each and every world, and within each and every atom.

“Mañjuśrī! That is to say, within as many bodies of Tathāgatas as there are, they speak of that many bodhisattva practices; that many Tathāgatas’ invisible-crest marks; all their various marks, and within each mark, all their secondary characteristics; within each secondary characteristic, all their pores; and within each pore, from moment to moment, they constantly emit great oceans of light rays, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*). Some constantly emit great oceans of light rays adorned with merits as numerous as the atoms in all worlds and incalculable;
some constantly emit great oceans of light rays adorned with incalculable wisdom and merit.”
Some constantly emit great oceans of light on the *pāramitās*, numbering as many as incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*);
some constantly emit great oceans of light on the stages of dwelling (*bhūmi*), numbering as many as incalculable;
and some constantly emit great oceans of light on the *dhāraṇīs*, numbering as many as incalculable.
Some constantly emit great oceans of light of incalculable liberations;
some constantly emit great oceans of light of incalculable unimpeded eloquence and joy in teaching;
and some constantly emit great oceans of light of incalculable great vows.
Some constantly emit great oceans of light that bring immeasurable beings to peace and security;
some constantly emit great oceans of light that cause immeasurable beings to enter the bodhisattva practices;
and some constantly emit great oceans of light that cause immeasurable beings to enter the state of a Tathāgata.
Some constantly emit an incalculable number of great oceans of light that cause sentient beings to enter into accordance with their mental activities;
some constantly emit an incalculable number of great oceans of light that cause them to enter into worlds;
and some constantly emit an incalculable number of great oceans of light that cause them to enter into eons.
Some constantly emit an incalculable ocean of light that causes entry into the exposition of the three periods of time;
others constantly emit an incalculable ocean of light that causes entry into the mind of tirelessness.

“Mañjuśrī! In this way, there constantly issues forth a great ocean of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lights; a great ocean of non-discriminative wisdom that is unobstructed, unimpeded, and without distinction, pervading the entirety of space and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), without limit, remaining and sustaining itself through kalpas to transform sentient beings, without any fear.”

“Mañjuśrī! Such are the inconceivable deeds of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas: throughout the ten directions, in all the great oceans of worlds, they simultaneously teach and transform the great ocean of sentient beings, moment by moment.”
There are oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the wisdom of various explanations of the great ocean adorned with incalculable and diverse merits;
there are oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the wisdom of various explanations of the great ocean adorned with incalculable and diverse wisdom-merits;
and there are oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the wisdom of various explanations of the great ocean of incalculable and diverse *pāramitās*.
There are oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the wisdom of variously expounding the great ocean of incalculable, diverse samādhis;
there are oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the wisdom of variously expounding the great ocean of incalculable, diverse liberations;
and there are oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the wisdom of variously expounding the great ocean of incalculable, diverse, unimpeded eloquence.
There may be oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the ocean of various and distinct superknowledges and the wisdom of various and distinct explanations;
there may be oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the ocean of various and distinct great vows and the wisdom of various and distinct explanations;
there may be oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the ocean of various and distinct exertions of diligence and the wisdom of various and distinct explanations.
There are oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the wisdom of variously expounding the great ocean of attaining peace through incalculable and diverse ways;
there are oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the wisdom of variously expounding the great ocean of entering the bodhisattva practices through incalculable and diverse ways;
and there are oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the wisdom of variously expounding the great ocean of the Tathāgata through incalculable and diverse ways.

There are oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the wisdom of various discourses that lead them into the ocean of the mental activities of sentient beings through incalculably diverse ways;
there are oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the wisdom of various discourses that lead them into the ocean of worlds through incalculably diverse ways;
and there are oceans of sentient beings whom he teaches by means of the wisdom of various discourses that lead them into the ocean of eons through incalculably diverse ways.
“In this way, there may be oceans of sentient beings whom one causes to enter the three periods of time;
there may be oceans of sentient beings whom one causes to enter the teachings of the three periods of time;
and there may be oceans of sentient beings whom one causes to enter the mind of tirelessness.”
There may be oceans of sentient beings whom he causes to enter the wisdom of non-differentiation;
there may be oceans of sentient beings whom he causes to enter the wisdom of heroic prowess;
there may be oceans of sentient beings whom he causes to enter the wisdom of heroic prowess regarding buddha-lands.
There may be oceans of sentient beings whom one causes to enter the ocean of the power of swift mastery;
there may be oceans of sentient beings whom one causes to enter the ocean of the power of swift mastery of the body;
there may be oceans of sentient beings whom one causes to enter the ocean of the power of swift mastery of vows.
There may be oceans of sentient beings whom he causes to enter the wisdom of the mastery of realms;
there may be oceans of sentient beings whom he causes to enter the wisdom of the mastery of knowledge;
there may be oceans of sentient beings whom he causes to enter the wisdom of the mastery of supernormal powers.
There may be oceans of sentient beings whom he causes to enter the power of the "Vigorous Intellect.

Thus, in every thought-moment, for oceans of sentient beings as numerous as all atoms and as numerous as various other atoms, he teaches and transforms them through incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) and diverse modes of intellectual exposition.

“Mañjuśrī! This is a brief explanation of how the Buddhas thus teach and transform sentient beings without fear; were it to be explained in detail, even if one were to remain for as many eons as there are until the end of the future, they could not be fully described.”

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were good sons or good daughters who, for as many sentient beings as there are atoms in all worlds, daily provided and made offerings of celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, as well as celestial clothing, bedding, and medicinal decoctions; and suppose they continued to provide and make such offerings for as many oceans of eons as there are atoms in world-systems numbering as many as the sands of an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Ganges River.

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there should be a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, toward a single upāsaka who does not believe in other deities and who maintains the ten paths of wholesome action, conceives such a thought as to embrace that person and, for even a single day, bestows upon them a single meal—this is one who studies the various precepts and practices of the Buddha.
“Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!”

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, throughout as many world-systems as there are atoms of dust, do not believe in other honored ones, but uphold the ten paths of wholesome action; and if these upāsakas were to daily provide offerings and support with celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, along with celestial robes, bedding, and medicinal decoctions, continuing in this manner for oceans of kalpas equal in number to the atoms of dust in as many worlds as there are sands in incalculable Ganges Rivers—[if they were to do so]...
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who takes up a single bhikṣu and provides him with even a single meal for as little as one day.
“Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!”

If there were a son or daughter of good family who, for as many monks as there are atoms in all worlds, daily provided offerings of celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, along with celestial clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites—continuing in this manner for an ocean of eons equal in number to the atoms in world-systems as numerous as the sands of an *asaṃkhyeya* of Ganges Rivers.
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who takes up another person who practices with faith and, for even a single day, bestows upon them a single meal.
“Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!”

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for as many kalpa-oceans as there are atoms in worlds numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges—up to an incalculable number (asaṃkhyeya)—daily provide offerings and support to all those practitioners of faith, providing them with celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, celestial garments, bedding, and medicinal elixirs; and if they continue to do so in this manner for that many kalpa-oceans.
Mañjuśrī! If there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, for even a single day, takes up a practitioner of the Dharma and bestows upon them a single meal;
“Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!”

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for as many kalpa-oceans as there are atoms in worlds numbering as many as the atoms in all worlds, daily provide and offer celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, along with celestial clothing, bedding, and medicinal elixirs, to practitioners of the Dharma whose number is equal to the atoms in those worlds.
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for even a single day, takes up one person from among eight people and gives them a single meal.
Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for as many eons as there are atoms in worlds numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges—up to an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) number of such oceans of eons—daily provide offerings and support to as many *aṣṭamaka* (persons on the eighth stage) as there are atoms in all worlds, by means of celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, celestial food and drink, celestial clothing, bedding, and medicinal decoctions; [if they do so]...

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for even a single day, takes up a person who is a candidate for the first fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattipratipannaka) and offers them a single meal.
“Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!”

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for as many eons as there are atoms in worlds as numerous as the sands of an incalculable number of Ganges Rivers, daily provide offerings of celestial ambrosia with a hundred flavors, as well as celestial clothing, bedding, and medicinal decoctions, to as many *srotāpanna-pratipannaka* (those entering the stream) as there are atoms in all worlds, and thus continue to make such offerings throughout that vast ocean of eons.

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there were another son of good family or daughter of good family who, for even a single day, were to provide a single meal as an offering to a single srotāpanna, having taken that person under their care;
Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, for as many kalpas as there are atoms in worlds numbering as many as the sands of an incalculable number of Ganges Rivers, daily provide and offer celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, along with celestial clothing, bedding, and medicinal decoctions, to as many Srotāpannas as there are atoms in all worlds.

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for even a single day, takes up a person who is a candidate for the stage of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and bestows upon them a single meal.
“Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!”

If there are good men or good women who, for as many kalpa-oceans as there are atoms in worlds numbering as many as the atoms in all worlds, daily provide offerings of celestial ambrosia with a hundred flavors, as well as celestial clothing, bedding, and medicinal decoctions, to those approaching the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin, making such offerings throughout a period equal to the number of atoms in worlds as numerous as the sands of incalculable Ganges Rivers.

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there is another son of good family or daughter of good family who, for even a single day, takes up a single Sakṛdāgāmin and bestows upon that person a single meal as an offering.
Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for as many kalpa-oceans as there are atoms in worlds numbering as many as the sands of an *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges River, daily provide offerings and support to Pratyekabuddhas (Sakṛdāgāmins) by presenting them with celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, as well as celestial garments, bedding, and medicinal decoctions.

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for even a single day, takes up a person who is a candidate for the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmipratipannaka) and offers them a single meal.
“Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!”

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for as many kalpa-oceans as there are atoms in worlds numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges—up to an incalculable number (asaṃkhyeya)—daily provide offerings and support to as many individuals on the path to the stage of non-returner (anāgāmin) as there are atoms in all worlds, using celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, celestial food and drink, celestial garments, bedding, and medicinal decoctions; and if they continue to make such offerings in this manner throughout those oceans of kalpas.
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for even a single day, takes up one person who is an Anāgāmin and bestows upon them a single meal.
Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for as many kalpa-oceans as there are atoms in worlds numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges—up to an incalculable number (asaṃkhyeya)—daily provide offerings and support to Anāgāmins as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, presenting them with celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, as well as celestial garments, bedding, and medicinal decoctions; and if they continue to make such offerings in this manner throughout those oceans of kalpas.

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for even a single day, takes up the care of a single arhat and bestows upon them a single meal as an offering.
“Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!”

If there were good sons or good daughters who, day after day, offered and provided celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, as well as celestial garments, bedding, and medicinal decoctions, to as many Arhats as there are atoms in all worlds—continuing such offerings for an ocean of eons equal in number to the atoms in worlds as numerous as the sands of incalculable Ganges Rivers.
Mañjuśrī! If there should be another son or daughter of good family who, for even a single day, takes up a Pratyekabuddha and offers him a single meal;
Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas. Mañjuśrī!

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for as many Pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in all worlds, daily provide offerings of celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, along with celestial garments, bedding, and medicinal decoctions, continuing such worship and support for as many oceans of eons as there are atoms in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there are good men or good women who see an image of the Buddha painted on a wall, or see an image of the Buddha within a scripture case.
Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
How much more so if one joins the palms, or offers even a single flower to a Buddha image, or a single incense stick, or powdered incense, or unguent, or lights a single lamp?
Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Śrāvaka Saṃghas as there are in worlds equal in number to the sands of one Ganges River, daily offer and provide sustenance with celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, as well as celestial garments, bedding, and medicinal decoctions—continuing in this manner for oceans of kalpas equal in number to the atoms within worlds as countless as the sands of immeasurable, boundless asaṃkhyeya Ganges Rivers.

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for even a single day, provides coarse food and drink as a gift to a single bodhisattva practicing the sheep-cart vehicle who possesses a straightforward mind and whose single root of goodness can serve as the seed for Buddhahood, thereby embracing that bodhisattva—[this merit is far greater].
"Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!"

If there were good sons or good daughters who, for as many eons as there are atoms in worlds as numerous as the sands of an incalculable number of Ganges Rivers, daily provided offerings and support to Bodhisattvas practicing the sheep-cart vehicle—equal in number to the atoms in all worlds—by presenting them with celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, as well as celestial garments, bedding, and medicinal decoctions.

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for even a single day, provides a single meal as an offering to a person practicing the bodhisattva path on an elephant vehicle—whoever possesses even a single root of goodness capable of becoming the seed of a Buddha—and thereby takes that person under their care; [the merit of this is immeasurable].
Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!

If there were good sons or good daughters who, for as many kalpas as there are atoms in worlds numbering as many as the atoms in all worlds, daily provided and made offerings of celestial ambrosia of a hundred flavors, as well as celestial clothing, bedding, and medicinal decoctions, to bodhisattvas practicing the elephant-vehicle path, whose number was equal to the atoms in those worlds; and if they continued to provide such offerings in this manner for an ocean of kalpas equal in number to the atoms in worlds as numerous as the sands of an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Ganges River—[the merit derived from this would be surpassed by that of one who upholds this sutra].
Mañjuśrī! If there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who,

for even a single day, takes up a person of the bodhisattva lineage who practices the vehicle of the sun and moon and has planted roots of merit in the Buddha, and provides that person with a single meal.
Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas.

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were good sons or good daughters who, for as many kalpa-oceans as there are atoms in worlds numbering as many as the atoms in all worlds, daily provided offerings of celestial ambrosia with a hundred flavors, as well as celestial garments, bedding, and medicinal decoctions, to Bodhisattvas as numerous as the suns and moons moving through those worlds. They would thus provide such offerings and support for them throughout those oceans of kalpas.”

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for even a single day, takes up a bodhisattva who possesses the supernormal powers of the Śrāvaka vehicle and offers them a single meal.
“Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!”

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for as many eons as there are atoms in worlds numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges—up to an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*)—daily provide and offer divine ambrosia of a hundred flavors, along with celestial garments, bedding, and medicinal decoctions, to Bodhisattvas who possess supernatural powers and belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds.

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for even a single day, takes up a bodhisattva who possesses the supernormal powers of a Tathāgata and offers them a single meal;
“Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!”

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for as many kalpa-oceans as there are atoms in worlds numbering as many as the Ganges-sands of asaṃkhyeyas, daily provide offerings and support to bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who possess the spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms of all worlds—offering them celestial ambrosia with a hundred flavors, as well as celestial clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there are good men or good women who, regarding this Dharma-gate, are able to write it themselves or cause others to write it;
Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas. Mañjuśrī!
The same should be said regarding the offenses of unwholesome karma; one should understand this well. “Mañjuśrī!

In this way, those who practice by means of the sheep vehicle, the elephant vehicle, the sun and moon vehicles, or those who practice the supernormal powers of the Śrāvaka vehicle—even Bodhisattvas—cause beings in the animal realm to give rise to roots of goodness.”
If a man or a woman gives rise to even a slight thought of anger such that their facial expression changes, they obstruct a single root of goodness even in an animal;
Mañjuśrī, this transgression is infinitely more grave than the former, beyond measure, beyond calculation.

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were a man or a woman who, in the worlds of the ten directions, plucked out the eyes of all sentient beings—as numerous as the atoms in every world—and plundered all their necessities of life and wealth.
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there should be a man or a woman who, toward a single bodhisattva, gives rise to a mind of contempt and arrogance, reviling, insulting, and disparaging them.
Mañjuśrī! This transgression exceeds the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!

If there are men or women who, toward even a single bodhisattva, for any reason whatsoever—even on account of something as slight as this—speak abusively, revile, or disparage them with a mind of deceit and arrogance.

Those men and women fall into the Great Screaming Hell, where their bodies are five hundred *yojanas* in height and breadth. They have five hundred heads; on each head there are five hundred mouths; in each mouth there are five hundred tongues; and upon each tongue there are five hundred plows with which their tongues are furrowed.

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were a man or a woman who, with blades and clubs, slaughtered all the sentient beings within the trichiliocosm and plundered all their means of livelihood and material wealth.
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there should be a man or a woman who conceives a mind of contempt and pride toward a bodhisattva, giving rise to thoughts of anger and resentment. Mañjuśrī!
This sin exceeds the former by immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. "Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were a man or a woman who, conceiving an evil mind and failing to give rise to a mind of peace and security for sentient beings, were to kill all the *arhats*—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—in every single Jambudvīpa within every single world-system throughout as many worlds as there are sands in the Ganges; and suppose they were to do so until all such *arhats* had been completely destroyed."

The stūpas and temples made of the seven treasures belonging to as many Buddhas and Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, along with their jeweled railings, banners, pennants, and canopies—all were utterly destroyed and completely annihilated.

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there be any man or woman who, toward a bodhisattva who has faith in the Mahāyāna—even one who is but slightly so—gives rise to a mind of contempt and pride for any reason whatsoever, and reviles or slanders them with anger;
Mañjuśrī! This transgression exceeds the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Why is this?
Because it is from the Bodhisattvas that all Buddhas are born, and because it is through the Bodhisattvas that the lineage of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, remains unbroken.
If there is anyone who slanders the Bodhisattvas, such a person is said to be slandering the Buddha and slandering the Dharma.
Why is this? Because there is no bodhisattva apart from the Dharma, and because all bodhisattvas are themselves the Dharma. "Mañjuśrī!..."
If there are men or women who, with a mind of hatred toward all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, bind them and place them in the dark hells.
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore,
if there should be a man or a woman who feels anger toward a bodhisattva, even for as long as it takes to turn their body away and look in another direction— Mañjuśrī!
This transgression exceeds the former by immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. "Mañjuśrī!
Suppose there were a man or woman who were to completely seize all the necessities of life and all the wealth belonging to every sentient being throughout the entire Jambudvīpa."
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there should be a man or a woman who, toward any bodhisattva—whether that bodhisattva be good or evil—with a mind of resentment, reviles, insults, or disparages them.
"Mañjuśrī! This transgression exceeds the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!"
For example, just as Sumeru, the King of Mountains, surpasses all other mountains in its radiant brilliance— surpassing them in terms of height, depth, breadth, and width— so too, Mañjuśrī,

a bodhisattva who has faith in this Dharma-gate is the most excellent and supreme among all the bodhisattvas in the worlds of the ten directions, numbering as many as the atoms within all those worlds.

Why is this? If there is a bodhisattva who believes in this Dharma-gate, the merit arising from the five pāramitās and all roots of goodness cultivated over incalculable eons—compared to believing in this Dharma-gate, the latter’s merit is superior.
What is meant by "superior" refers to its height, depth, breadth, and extent.
“Mañjuśrī! If there were good sons or good daughters who caused as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in the worlds of the ten directions to resolve upon the mind of enlightenment;”
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there are sons or daughters of good family who believe that this Dharma-gate is a supramundane Dharma, Mañjuśrī!
This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* factors. "Mañjuśrī!
If there are good sons or good daughters who cause all sentient beings to have faith in this Dharma-gate and lead them to resolve upon Bodhicitta..."

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there are good men or good women who believe in this Dharma-gate, and having believed, they write it down, or cause others to write it, or recite it themselves, or teach others to recite it, or even if they merely write it in a scripture-casket with faith and reverence, uphold it, make offerings to it, and present lamps, incense, flowers, powdered incense, unguents, and flower garlands as offerings to this Dharma-gate—[they shall obtain immeasurable merit].
“Mañjuśrī! This merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Mañjuśrī!”

If there are sons or daughters of good family who cause all sentient beings throughout all worlds who believe in the path of the śrāvakas to sever and extinguish every single one of those śrāvaka-path beings' roots of goodness for dwelling as immeasurable asaṃkhyeya cakravartin kings, as well as their superior and wondrous roots of goodness for being born in the heavens.
Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were another person who obstructed a single root of goodness in a single bodhisattva mahāsattva. Mañjuśrī!
This transgression is immeasurable and incalculably greater than the former; how much more so for one who, out of anger, reviles, insults, and slanders them? "Mañjuśrī!
If there were a man or a woman who destroyed and burned as many stūpas and shrines of the Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River..."

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there should be a man or a woman who gives rise to a mind of anger toward sentient beings who are bodhisattvas faithful in the Mahāyāna, and reviles, insults, or disparages them.
Mañjuśrī! This transgression exceeds the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Why is this?
Because it is from the Bodhisattvas that all Buddhas are born; because it is from the Buddhas that there are stūpas and temples;
and because it is by reason of the Buddha that there exist all the devas and humans of the world.
Therefore, to make offerings to the bodhisattvas is to make offerings to all the Tathāgatas;
if there are those who make offerings to the bodhisattvas, they are making offerings to the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
to revile a bodhisattva is to revile the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
“Mañjuśrī! If there are good men or good women who wish to rely upon the unsurpassed offering to all Tathāgatas, they should make offerings to all Bodhisattvas.”

“Mañjuśrī! In any city, town, or village, there may be one hundred million, or one thousand million, or one hundred thousand million, or even immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) bodhisattvas who do not give rise to faith in this Dharma-gate.”
Those bodhisattvas may encounter disturbances caused by kings, or disturbances caused by karma, or calamities of water, or perils of precipices, or calamities of fire, or perils of bandits.

Furthermore, within those cities, towns, and villages, there may be a bodhisattva who has faith in this Dharma-gate; even if that bodhisattva possesses incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) karmic offenses, they shall all be completely extinguished and they will be far removed from all calamities.

However, within those cities, towns, and villages, this bodhisattva encounters no danger from kings, no danger from karma, no danger from water, no danger from precipices, no danger from fire, no danger from thieves, and no danger from malicious beings who lack faith in the Dharma.

If a bodhisattva has faith in this dharma-gate, all their accumulated offenses from incalculable eons—which would otherwise lead to rebirth in the hells, as animals, or as hungry ghosts—are extinguished in this very life.

Yet, those bodhisattvas who possess the extremely heavy karmic offenses of the Avīci Hell for incalculable and ineffable eons will have them extinguished in their very present body; all such difficulties shall be entirely eliminated. Even if they possess the extremely heavy karmic offenses of the Avīci Hell for ten, twenty, or thirty eons, these shall all be extinguished within this very life.
Why is this? Because they have accumulated a great mass of merit. "Mañjuśrī!..."

Suppose there were a great pond, one hundred yojanas in width, and the water within that pond possessed the eight excellent qualities; if someone were to place even a single *pala* of poison—or even a thousand *kārṣāpaṇas*—into that pond, there would be no trace of its poisonous vapor.
Why is this? Because it has obtained great water and gathered it in abundance. Mañjuśrī!

Thus, although there may be immeasurable and boundless evil karmic offenses that ought to cause one to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts for a full kalpa, they will be immediately extinguished.
"Why is this? Because faith in this Dharma-gate possesses great merit that is immeasurable and boundless.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this Dharma-gate, the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had come from the worlds of the ten directions, the great assembly, and all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Scripture on the Dharma-Door of Entering the Seal through the Power of Faith, Scroll Five.
